cim: An AI apprenticeship programme seeks to empower international agency staff amid job cuts
cim_eredeti: An AI apprenticeship programme seeks to empower international agency staff amid job cuts
szoveg_eredeti:
A Geneva-funded programme is teaching staff at international organisations how to master artificial intelligence at a time when employees are under pressure to increase their performance due to job cuts. But workers remain circumspect about the tech’s impacts.

A year after international Geneva’s biggest budget shakeup, staff at organisations are still reeling from job cuts and uncertainty over their own positions as system-wide reforms take hold. An apprenticeship programme is providing AI skills to help staff as they cope with heavier workloads.

In early October, a small graduation ceremony took place on the top floor of an international agency building, offering spectacular views of Lake Geneva and nearby organisations. A couple of dozen employees working in the multilateral hub were awarded for completing a three-week course designed to help staff at agencies understand how artificial intelligence works, and teach them how to create their own AI tools to facilitate complex or time-consuming tasks.

“I feel extremely fortunate to have been selected,” Anna Jakowska Eriksson, a data analyst at the International Trade Centre (ITC), said, before receiving her diploma from Diplo, the organisation that organised the course funded by the Foundation for the Adaptation of International Geneva (Fagi), a public-private partnership aimed at helping struggling international organisations and NGOs. Diplo is focused on capacity building in the area of digital diplomacy and digital policy. Jakowska Eriksson explained how she learned how to build an AI tool called the TradeMap Navigator, which will allow two million ITC data users to find answers to questions sourced from its huge statistical international trade database. “We have a small team of people who regularly answer the exact same questions over and over about market analysis, about access to data, about interpreting indicators,” she said. “I built something that could provide quantitative and qualitative information, so that my colleagues could hopefully in the future have some time to do things that are more strategic and interesting.”

Another graduate was Abhinav Sharma, a human resources officer at the International Federation of the Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, who built an AI agent to serve as a staff guide, with information such as regulations for staff working in different countries uploaded. As an aid organisation having to quickly onboard additional staff during disasters, the agent will help staff access the information quickly, freeing up his department to focus on other tasks.

“Before joining the apprenticeship, AI was only about putting in the input and getting the output,” Sharma said. “With this programme, we learned about chunking, retrieval strategy and how you can drive your results if you build an agent.”

The founder of the apprenticeship, Jovan Kurbalija, a former diplomat, stressed that the course is taught “in the best spirit of Swiss vocational apprenticeship training”. He explained how his approach combined “hands-on technical practice with philosophical reflection, governance, and mentorship”.

Amid recent apocalyptic warnings from AI industry insiders, he also sought to debunk warnings on humanity’s inability to remain in control of the technology, instead providing the tools to create independent AI agents, to reduce hallucinations – AI-generated responses containing false, misleading or fabricated information – while reducing data security risks.

“You have to understand what is going on,” Kurbalija said. ”It is beyond just technology. It's beyond just governance. The course leads to the question of who we are, what is the meaning of our knowledge, and how knowledge defines us as humans, and how we can preserve it and enrich it for the future.”

According to Fagi, Diplo’s AI apprenticeship was the first pitch for funding received by the foundation in late 2025 and was awarded a budget of CHF1.25 million. The foundation has since supported other AI-related projects, including in peace and security.

Many organisations in Geneva, however, have only recently started using the technology in their work. Despite a vision by UN secretary general António Guterres to proactively adopt AI for its internal work in 2023, it was only adopted at UN agencies as recently as last year.

“It is very new and came as a surprise,” Séverine Deboos, representative of the International Labour Organization staff union, said, recalling when staff at the agency began using ChatGPT, under a dedicated licence, after a pilot project was launched in late 2025 and guidance on its use was developed.

“Staff view its use reluctantly, with trepidations that it will replace their work,” she explained, noting that its adoption came just as discussions over increasing efficiency and effectiveness at ILO coincided with its mounting budget crisis as member states failed to pay their dues.

Like at other UN agencies, Deboos says that there’s particular concern that junior staff roles, writing and preparing reports and transcripts, may be made redundant by AI. Some colleagues, she adds, have raised concerns over data protection, to which the administration has ensured that ILO operates within a “protected space”.

AI training, however, is not yet a priority for staff, she explained. “We are still trying to understand job cuts, and haven’t had the capacity to step back and look at the longer trends.”

Ian Richards, president of the UN staff association, regretted that while the organisation has long spoken about the importance of embracing AI globally to address global issues, resources to help its own staff keep up with tech developments have not materialised. Often, only limited access to Microsoft’s AI platform Copilot is provided, he said, with many employees having to pay out of their own pocket to access essential AI tools. Richards said that management’s argument that AI would compensate for lost jobs has not added up. A staff survey has shown that employees have had to work longer hours to fill gaps left by others no longer there.

He admitted that AI training was key. “Staff need to be up to date on the latest technology skills, because if you are not, you are not as competitive in the labour market,” he said.

For one linguist working at the World Meteorological Organization with no experience in AI, the Diplo programme provided her with just that expertise. “The linguistic assistant I built is helping me in my daily work, applying the rules I gave it,” she said. I do not feel replaced by this tool, but better equipped because it relies on my expertise.”
